tellings.quote: Solon, who was intending to use the tale for his poem, enquired into the meaning of the names, and found that the early Egyptians in writing them down had translated them into their own language, and he recovered the meaning of the several names and when copying them out again translated them into our language.
My great-grandfather, Dropides, had the original writing, which is still in my possession, and was carefully studied by me when I was a child.

In the Egyptian Delta, at the head of which the river Nile divides, there is a certain district which is called the district of Sais, and the great city of the district is also called Sais, and is the city from which King Amasis came. The citizens have a deity for their foundress; she is called in the Egyptian tongue Neith, and is asserted by them to be the same whom the Hellenes call Athene; they are great lovers of the Athenians, and say that they are in some way related to them.

To this city came Solon, and was received there with great honour; he asked the priests who were most skilful in such matters, about antiquity, and made the discovery that neither he nor any other Hellene knew anything worth mentioning about the times of old.
Thereupon one of the priests, who was of a very great age, said: O Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children, and there is not an old man among you.
if there were any actions noble or great or in any other way remarkable, they have all been written down by us of old, and are preserved in our temples.

As touching your citizens of 9000 years ago, I will briefly inform you of their laws and of their most famous action; the exact particulars of the whole we will hereafter go through at our leisure in the sacred registers themselves.

plain: The ancient Greek lawmaker Solon is said to have learned the story of Atlantis from Egyptian priests at a temple of the goddess Neith in Sais, a city in the Nile Delta. The writer Graham Hancock, who researches lost ancient civilizations, tells Michels this twice and draws only on Plato's account. The second time he adds that the priests read the hieroglyphs on the temple wall to Solon and translated them, and he dates the visit to about 600 BC and the events to about 9600 BC. The story comes from the Greek philosopher Plato's dialogues Timaeus and Critias, read here in Benjamin Jowett's translation. In them Solon 'was received there with great honour' at Sais, and a very old priest tells him, 'O Solon, Solon, you Hellenes are never anything but children.' The priest says great deeds 'have all been written down by us of old, and are preserved in our temples,' and speaks of 'your citizens of 9000 years ago,' saying the full particulars are in 'the sacred registers themselves.' In the text the priest tells the story himself and the written record is left to be read later. Whether that record was on a wall or in registers, and the picture of priests reading hieroglyphs aloud, are Hancock's details, which the text neither states nor excludes. In the Critias, Plato's speaker adds that Solon translated the Egyptian names into Greek and that his great-grandfather Dropides 'had the original writing.' The researcher Tim Alberino also brings up the priest of Sais teaching Solon, but he stresses the priest's lesson that the world is struck by cataclysms again and again, and ties it to our own age. If the story is true, a civilization far older than recorded history once existed and was lost.

discussion.text: In Jowett's translation of the Timaeus, the old priest at Sais tells Solon that the great deeds "have all been written down by us of old, and are preserved in our temples", the temple record the teller describes, and gives him the laws himself: "I will briefly describe them to you, and you shall read the account of them at your leisure in the sacred registers". In the text the priest tells the story and the record waits to be read later; whether it stood on a wall or in registers, and the picture of priests reading hieroglyphs aloud to Solon, are the teller's details, which the text neither states nor excludes.
